chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Samura ibn Jundub had a date-palm tree in the garden of a man from the Ansar, and the house of the Ansari was adjacent to the door of the garden, and he used to pass by it on his way to his palm tree without asking for permission, so the Ansari spoke to him about asking permission when he came, but Samura refused. So when he had refused, the Ansari came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and complained to him and informed him of the matter, so the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sent for him and informed him of what the Ansari had said and his complaint, and said: 'If you want to enter, ask permission,' but he refused. So when he had refused, he bargained with him until he increased the price to whatever Allah willed, but he continued to refuse to sell it, so he said: 'For it, you will get a palm tree to support you in Paradise,' but he refused to accept that. Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to the Ansari: 'Go and uproot it and throw it at him, for there is no harm nor causing harm [in Islam].'

key_terms.لا ضرر ولا ضرار: No harm and no causing harm (a fundamental legal maxim)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal principle of 'No Harm' (La Dara wa la Dirar) as demonstrated in the story of Samura ibn Jundub?
ai.summary: This narrative from Al-Kafi illustrates the practical application of the principle of 'La Dara wa la Dirar' (no harm and no causing harm) through the Prophet's (peace be upon him) resolution of a dispute between Samara ibn Jundub and an Ansari over a date palm and right of way. The Prophet's command to uproot the tree and throw it at the stubborn neighbor highlights that the removal of the source of harm is a valid legal remedy, emphasizing the precedence of preventing harm over maintaining property rights in cases of obstruction. This incident is frequently cited by Shia jurists to demonstrate how specific historical events establish general legal maxims in Islamic jurisprudence.
